compartments.name: Inputs
compartments.blurb: Nutrients, hormones, stresses and drugs — the information the cell is trying to read. Not a cellular location.
compartments.sensing_note: Amino acids are shown here as inputs, but they are sensed *inside* the cell: leucine by cytosolic Sestrin2, arginine by cytosolic CASTOR1 and by lysosomal SLC38A9, SAM by cytosolic SAMTOR.

compartments.name: Plasma membrane
compartments.blurb: Where receptors meet the outside world and where PIP3 is made. Akt has to come here to be switched on.

compartments.name: Cytosol
compartments.blurb: The mixing bowl. Most sensors, kinases and brakes live here and diffuse until they are recruited somewhere specific.

compartments.name: Lysosomal surface
compartments.blurb: The decision platform. mTORC1 is only switched on here, because this is the only place it meets Rheb. Everything about nutrient sensing is really about getting mTORC1 to this membrane.
compartments.sensing_note: Simplified on purpose: this band means 'the endomembrane surface where mTORC1 is switched on'. Rheb is not exclusively lysosomal — a large fraction sits on the ER and Golgi, and which pool activates mTORC1 is still argued. Rheb is drawn here because the lysosome is where it meets mTORC1, which is the fact the pathway logic turns on. The ER, Golgi and peroxisome are not drawn as separate bands.
compartments.headline: 6 of the 7 direct inputs to mTORC1 act on this membrane. The remainder is complex assembly, which builds mTORC1 rather than regulating it — so every direct regulator of mTORC1 activity in this model acts at the lysosome.

compartments.name: Nucleus
compartments.blurb: Where the slow, transcriptional arm of the pathway acts. Hours, not seconds.

compartments.name: Mitochondrion
compartments.blurb: Both a target of mTORC1 (biogenesis) and a source of the energy signal that AMPK reads.

compartments.name: Autophagy machinery
compartments.blurb: The recycling plant mTORC1 keeps switched off while nutrients last.

compartments.name: Biological outcomes
compartments.blurb: Cell-, tissue- and organism-level consequences. Not a cellular location — and the evidence here is a different kind of evidence from the molecular steps above.

Requires LKB1 (or CaMKK2) to be armed at all. LKB1-null cells cannot mount this response, which is why AMPK-dependence claims are cell-line specific.

nodes.label: mTORC1

Not a single on/off output. Rapamycin collapses S6K1 phosphorylation while sparing much of 4E-BP1, and TFEB phosphorylation depends on FLCN/RagC — so 'mTORC1 activity' depends on which substrate you measure.

interactions.mechanism: Leucine binds a pocket inside Sestrin2 with roughly 20 uM affinity - close to the concentration at which cells actually feel leucine coming and going. The bound sensor can no longer hold GATOR2, so leucine effectively switches the brake off.
interactions.boundary: Affinity was measured in vitro; whether the same 20 uM setpoint holds in tissues with different leucine transport is untested.

interactions.mechanism: When leucine is scarce, free Sestrin2 clamps onto GATOR2 and blocks it, keeping the whole pathway switched off.
Cytosolic arginine binds CASTOR1 and breaks its grip on GATOR2 - the same trick as leucine/Sestrin2, but for a different amino acid.
Arginine-free CASTOR1 binds GATOR2 and inhibits it, so the pathway stays off until arginine is available.
Released GATOR2 suppresses GATOR1 - a double negative. Two brakes in series is why the sensors can flip mTORC1 on so sharply.
interactions.teaching_note: Everyone agrees this inhibition happens; nobody has fully resolved how. Kept visible as an honest hole in a canonical pathway.
interactions.boundary: The epistasis is solid. VAL2022 resolved GATOR2's architecture by cryo-EM - a 1.1 MDa cage - and mapped where the sensors dock, but exactly how GATOR2 suppresses GATOR1's GAP activity is still not settled.
interactions.note: Good candidate for a 'mechanism gap' flag - textbook arrow, thin mechanistic evidence.

interactions.mechanism: KICSTOR is the dock that holds GATOR1 on the lysosomal surface. Without it, GATOR1 cannot reach its target and nutrient control of mTORC1 is lost.
GATOR1 acts as a GAP: it forces RagA/B to hydrolyse GTP, flipping the Rag heterodimer into the inactive shape that cannot hold mTORC1.
S-adenosylmethionine, the cell's methyl-donor currency, binds SAMTOR and pulls it off GATOR1 - this is how methionine availability reaches mTORC1.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge. Needs independent replication before it is treated as established.
interactions.note: Only one supporting study in the corpus - flag as thin.

interactions.mechanism: Methionine-starved SAMTOR binds the GATOR1-KICSTOR complex and helps it keep mTORC1 off.
interactions.note: Only one supporting study in the corpus.

interactions.mechanism: Ragulator both tethers the Rag GTPases to the lysosome and acts as their GEF, loading RagA/B with GTP - the active shape.
The lysosome's proton pump talks to Ragulator from the inside out: amino acids inside the lysosome change v-ATPase, which changes Ragulator, which changes the Rags.
interactions.boundary: The 'inside-out' model requires amino acids to accumulate inside the lysosome first; how they get there for every amino acid is not fully mapped.

interactions.mechanism: SLC38A9 sits in the lysosomal membrane and reads arginine on the inside, then signals sufficiency to the Rag complex; it also pumps essential amino acids, including leucine, back out into the cytosol.
interactions.note: Four independent studies - one of the best-supported edges in the sensor branch.

interactions.mechanism: FLCN-FNIP is the GAP for the other half of the Rag dimer (RagC/D). Only when both halves are in the right nucleotide state can the dimer hold mTORC1. Crucially this arm is SUBSTRATE-SPECIFIC: it gates TFEB and TFE3 phosphorylation, while canonical outputs like S6K1 and 4E-BP1 carry on without it.
interactions.teaching_note: Positive regulator of the RagC/D arm, despite being a tumour suppressor. It licenses mTORC1 to phosphorylate TFEB specifically — substrate choice, not overall activity.
interactions.boundary: The substrate selectivity is why Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is driven by constitutive nuclear TFEB/TFE3 rather than by blanket mTORC1 hyperactivation (NAP2020).

interactions.mechanism: The active Rag dimer grabs Raptor and physically drags mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface. This is a relocation, not an activation - the kinase is moved to where its activator waits.
interactions.teaching_note: Recruitment, not activation. The Rags decide *where* mTORC1 is; they do not switch the kinase on. This is why amino acids alone cannot drive growth.
interactions.note: The conceptual crux of the whole route: teach recruitment vs activation as two separate ideas.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 has to be on the lysosomal membrane to be switched on. Force it elsewhere and amino acids stop mattering.
interactions.teaching_note: A requirement, not a signal. The lysosome contributes a location.

interactions.mechanism: A competing model: the enzyme that loads leucine onto tRNA doubles as the leucine sensor, sensing charged leucine directly.
interactions.boundary: Proposed before the Sestrin2 model and never cleanly reconciled with it.
interactions.note: CONTESTED with LEU-SESN2. Two published leucine sensors, both from strong labs, never resolved head-to-head. Prime Contradiction Engine seed.

interactions.mechanism: In this model LARS acts as a GAP for RagD, doing for the RagC/D half what FLCN does - an alternative route from leucine to the Rags.
interactions.note: See LEU-LARS.

interactions.mechanism: Glutamine feeds mTORC1 partly by being burned into alpha-ketoglutarate; in some cells it activates mTORC1 without the Rags at all.
interactions.boundary: Rag-dependence differs between studies and cell types - JEW2015 explicitly reports a Rag-independent route.
interactions.note: Not a contradiction so much as a boundary condition: the sign is the same, the required machinery is not.

interactions.mechanism: Insulin and IGF-1 dock on their receptor, which recruits IRS proteins and switches on PI3K to make the lipid messenger PIP3.
PIP3 pulls Akt to the membrane, where it gets phosphorylated and activated.
interactions.teaching_note: Indirect on purpose: PI3K makes PIP3, and PIP3 recruits Akt. Recruitment then enables two separate phosphorylations. Three distinct events often drawn as one arrow.
interactions.context_note: PIP3 recruits Akt; recruitment alone does not activate it. Full activation additionally needs PDK1 (T308) and mTORC2 (S473), so the strength of this link depends on the activity of both of those.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC2 puts the second, activating phosphate on Akt (Ser473). This is the step rapamycin eventually breaks - and the reason chronic rapamycin causes metabolic side effects.
interactions.context_note: S473 contribution to Akt output is substrate-dependent: some Akt substrates are strongly mTORC2-dependent, others barely.
interactions.note: Bridge edge between the growth-factor route and the rapamycin route.

interactions.mechanism: Akt phosphorylates TSC2, disabling the complex. Growth-factor signalling works by removing a brake, not by pressing an accelerator.
TBC1D7 is the third, often-forgotten subunit of the TSC complex; losing it weakens the brake without removing it.
TSC2 is a GAP for Rheb: it forces Rheb to hydrolyse its GTP, switching it off. This is the single step where the tumour-suppressor function lives.
GTP-loaded Rheb binds mTORC1 at the lysosome and physically re-shapes its active site into the working conformation.
interactions.teaching_note: This is the actual on-switch. Everything the growth-factor arm does converges here.
interactions.context_note: Rheb must be GTP-loaded and co-located with mTORC1. Rheb is also distributed across the ER and Golgi, and which pool supplies the activating Rheb is unresolved.
interactions.note: Convergence point: the amino-acid route delivers mTORC1 here, the growth-factor route delivers Rheb. Both required.

interactions.mechanism: Akt phosphorylates PRAS40, which then gets sequestered away from mTORC1 - a second, parallel way insulin lifts a brake.
Unphosphorylated PRAS40 sits in the substrate groove of mTORC1 and blocks it - a built-in plug.
When energy runs low, AMPK phosphorylates TSC2 and strengthens the brake on Rheb.
interactions.context_note: Relative weight of this arm is cell-type dependent. AMPK reaches mTORC1 two ways — activating TSC2 and directly phosphorylating Raptor — and TSC2-null cells still suppress mTORC1 under energy stress, so the TSC2 arm is not universally the dominant one. Which arm carries the signal depends on TSC status, LKB1 status and the severity and duration of the energy stress.

interactions.mechanism: AMPK also hits mTORC1 directly by phosphorylating Raptor, imposing a metabolic checkpoint independent of TSC.
interactions.context_note: The Raptor arm is the TSC2-independent route, which is why it is measurable in TSC-null cells. Its relative contribution versus the TSC2 arm varies by cell type and by how deep the energy stress is.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises Grb10 - the start of a feedback loop that talks back to the insulin receptor.
Stabilised Grb10 damps insulin/IGF-1 receptor signalling. This is why blocking mTOR paradoxically raises Akt activity - remove mTORC1 and you remove its own brake on the receptor.
interactions.note: Explains a clinically important paradox; strong teaching edge.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 phosphorylates S6K1, switching on the translation machinery. This is the classic rapamycin-sensitive output and the readout most papers actually measure.
interactions.boundary: Caution: p-S6K is a proxy, not the phenotype. Many 'mTORC1 activity' claims rest on this single band.
interactions.context_note: Standard mTORC1 readout, but a readout is not the whole output. S6K1 phosphorylation is fully rapamycin-sensitive while 4E-BP1 is not, so 'mTORC1 activity' measured by S6K1 alone systematically overstates how much rapamycin inhibits mTORC1.
interactions.note: Worth flagging on the page: readout != outcome.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1, which lets go of eIF4E and frees cap-dependent translation. Rapamycin blocks this arm only partially - the origin of the whole 'rapamycin-resistant output' problem.
interactions.teaching_note: The sign is on 4E-BP1's repressor function: mTORC1 phosphorylates it, which stops it repressing eIF4E. Phosphorylation is not the same as inhibition — here it happens to be.

interactions.mechanism: Active mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 at an inhibitory site, holding autophagy shut while nutrients are plentiful.
Freed ULK1 nucleates the autophagosome - the self-eating programme that recycles damaged parts and is the leading candidate mechanism for mTOR inhibition's benefits.
Rapamycin is not an ordinary inhibitor: it first binds the small protein FKBP12, and only the two-part complex is the real drug.
interactions.note: The molecular-glue concept - genuinely surprising to newcomers.

interactions.mechanism: The rapamycin-FKBP12 complex wedges into the FRB site next to mTOR's active site, blocking access for some substrates but not all. That partial blockade is the whole story of the drug.
interactions.teaching_note: Partial, not complete. The FKBP12–rapamycin complex occludes the substrate channel, so S6K1 phosphorylation collapses while 4E-BP1 phosphorylation persists. This one fact created the entire ATP-competitive inhibitor field.

interactions.mechanism: Raptor is the subunit that defines mTORC1 and presents substrates to the kinase.
Rictor defines the second complex, mTORC2, which rapamycin does not block acutely.
Rapamycin does not touch mTORC2 in the short term - but over days it traps free mTOR and prevents new mTORC2 from being assembled.
interactions.boundary: Strictly time- and cell-type-dependent: absent acutely, present after prolonged exposure, and the sensitivity varies between cell lines. Treating this edge as unconditional is a common error.
interactions.note: THE key context-dependent edge. Should render dashed with an explicit 'chronic only' label.

interactions.mechanism: Losing mTORC2 uncouples Akt from insulin signalling and produces glucose intolerance - and this is separable from the lifespan benefit.
interactions.boundary: In mice, intermittent dosing largely spared glucose tolerance while keeping mTORC1 inhibition (ARR2015); not tested against this endpoint in humans.
interactions.note: Feeds hypothesis H2 in Knowledge_Gaps.

interactions.mechanism: Rapamycin extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice even when started late in life - the single most influential result in the geroscience arm of this Atlas.
interactions.boundary: Mouse only. No human lifespan or healthspan endpoint exists; EVERLAST has no results yet. BIT2016 shows a non-continuous schedule can still extend post-treatment life expectancy (males +60%, no female benefit). ARR2015 was removed from this edge: it measured side effects only.
interactions.note: Tier C. Do not let the arrow imply a human claim.

interactions.mechanism: Lowering mTORC1 activity extends lifespan across yeast, worms, flies and mice - the most conserved intervention in ageing biology.
interactions.boundary: No human hard-endpoint evidence. This is the Atlas's flagged 'human endpoint desert'.
interactions.context_note: Strongly modified by sex, strain, diet and the age at which inhibition starts. Effect direction is reproducible; effect size is not transferable between models.
interactions.note: Links to ATLAS_FINDINGS human-endpoint desert.

interactions.mechanism: Unphosphorylated 4E-BP1 clamps onto eIF4E and stops it assembling the cap-binding complex. mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 to release that grip - so the brake on translation is released, not the accelerator pressed.
Free eIF4E recruits the ribosome to the mRNA cap. This is the step that actually turns a growth signal into new protein.
interactions.note: Not every mRNA is equally sensitive - HSI2012 shows a specific translational program, not a uniform increase.

interactions.mechanism: S6K1 tags PDCD4 for destruction. PDCD4 is itself a translation inhibitor, so removing it is a second, parallel way mTORC1 lifts a brake on protein synthesis.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.
interactions.note: Thin - one supporting study.

interactions.mechanism: PDCD4 blocks the eIF4A helicase, so mRNAs with structured 5' ends cannot be unwound and translated.
Sustained cap-dependent translation is what physically builds muscle. Blocking mTOR in humans blunts the protein-synthesis response to exercise.
interactions.boundary: DRU2009 is direct human evidence: rapamycin blocked the contraction-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis in volunteers.
interactions.context_note: Requires mechanical load. mTORC1 activation without loading does not reproduce healthy hypertrophy, and constitutive activation alone is not sufficient.
interactions.note: Rare non-D badge in the output branch - DRU2009 is tier B.

interactions.mechanism: Active mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB right on the lysosomal surface, trapping it in the cytoplasm. Switch mTORC1 off and TFEB walks into the nucleus.
interactions.context_note: Substrate-selective. Depends on FLCN/FNIP RagC/D status, so mTORC1 can be active on S6K1 while not phosphorylating TFEB.
interactions.note: Four independent studies - one of the best-supported output edges.

interactions.mechanism: In the nucleus TFEB switches on a whole gene programme for autophagy and for building new lysosomes - the cell's recycling capacity, not just a single step.
interactions.note: The transcriptional arm of autophagy, distinct from the fast ULK1 arm.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 drives the SREBP transcription factors, which turn on the genes for making fat and cholesterol - growth needs membrane, not just protein.
SREBP is the master switch for de novo lipogenesis.
mTORC1 raises mitochondrial output two ways: through a YY1-PGC-1alpha transcription complex, and by relieving 4E-BP so mitochondrial proteins get translated.
The 4E-BP arm is specifically the one that gates mitochondrial protein translation - which is why this branch survives rapamycin better than the S6K arm.
mTORC1 couples nucleotide supply to demand - it turns on purine synthesis through the mitochondrial tetrahydrofolate cycle so a dividing cell can actually copy its DNA.
S6K1 phosphorylates CAD, the enzyme that starts de novo pyrimidine synthesis - a direct line from growth signal to DNA building blocks.

Keeping 4E-BP active extends lifespan under dietary restriction in flies, by preserving mitochondrial activity. One of the few places where a single downstream node, not the whole pathway, carries the lifespan effect.
interactions.boundary: Fly only, and only under dietary restriction - the effect was not seen on a full diet.
interactions.note: Boundary condition matters more than the headline here.

interactions.mechanism: Deleting S6K1 extends lifespan in mice and protects against diet-induced obesity - the clearest evidence that one downstream branch, not mTORC1 as a whole, carries much of the ageing signal.
interactions.boundary: Female mice only in SEL2009 - the lifespan extension was not significant in males.
interactions.note: Feeds the sex-dimorphism hypothesis H6 in Knowledge_Gaps.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 drives the inflammatory secretory programme of senescent cells, so inhibiting it makes old cells less toxic to their neighbours without necessarily killing them.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.
interactions.note: Thin - one supporting study.

interactions.mechanism: When ATP runs down, AMP builds up and switches AMPK on. AMPK is the cell's low-fuel sensor, and mTORC1 is one of the first things it shuts off.
LKB1 is the kinase that primes AMPK, phosphorylating AMPK-alpha directly on Thr172; without it the whole energy-stress arm is deaf.
interactions.boundary: Canonical step, established in LKB1-null cells and in vitro kinase assays (SHW2004).
interactions.note: Thin - one supporting study, and it is about the consequences of deficiency rather than the activation step itself.

interactions.mechanism: Metformin shifts the cell's energy balance and AMPK switches on - the route it is usually credited to, and why it keeps appearing next to rapamycin in longevity discussions.
interactions.boundary: How much of metformin's effect actually runs through AMPK is disputed: it still suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis in AMPK-null and LKB1-null mouse liver (FOR2010) and still inhibits mTORC1 in AMPK-null cells (KAL2010). See the parallel METFORMIN-MTORC1 edge.

interactions.mechanism: AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 at sites distinct from mTORC1's inhibitory one - so low energy switches autophagy on directly, not only by releasing the mTORC1 brake.
interactions.note: Two opposing inputs land on the same protein: this is where the pathway does arithmetic, not just relay.

interactions.mechanism: ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK back, damping the signal that activated it - a negative feedback loop that stops autophagy running away.
interactions.teaching_note: Closes the loop. ULK1 dampens the very kinase that activated it, so 'AMPK switches on autophagy' is a loop, not an arrow.
interactions.context_note: Closes a loop rather than acting as a one-way arrow; steady-state behaviour depends on the relative strength of both directions.

interactions.mechanism: Low oxygen induces REDD1 within minutes - a transcriptional response, so it is slower than AMPK but longer-lasting.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.
interactions.note: Thin - one supporting study.

interactions.mechanism: REDD1 works through the TSC complex, not around it - hypoxia and growth factors therefore converge on the same brake.
Many different stresses do the same physical thing: they drag TSC2 onto the lysosome, right where Rheb is. That relocation, not a change in TSC2 amount, is the switch.
interactions.teaching_note: Regulation by relocation: energy stress moves the TSC complex to the lysosome, where Rheb is. Location is a form of control the pathway uses repeatedly.
interactions.note: Nice parallel to RAG-MTORC1 in the amino-acid route: both branches work by moving a protein to the lysosome.

interactions.mechanism: The integrated stress response switches on Salr, a growth inhibitor - a route into mTORC1 that bypasses TSC and AMPK entirely.
interactions.boundary: Fly only, and newly reported.
interactions.note: Thin and species-limited, but it is a genuinely different input route - worth showing as such.

interactions.mechanism: Salr suppresses mTORC1-driven growth downstream of stress signalling.
The LKB1-AMPK axis keeps damaged mitochondria being cleared; lose it and mitochondrial DNA leaks into the cytosol and inflames the cell.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus (ZHU2026), and that study is a toxicology model rather than a dedicated test of this step. Treat as indicative.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC2 is built around the same mTOR kinase as mTORC1 - the partner subunits, not the catalytic core, are what make the two complexes different.
interactions.note: Three independent structures - unusually well supported for this corpus.

interactions.mechanism: SIN1 holds the complex together and positions the substrate; without it mTORC2 cannot phosphorylate Akt.
mLST8 is dispensable for mTORC1 in vivo but essential for mTORC2 - a rare clean genetic separation of the two complexes.
interactions.note: The cleanest genetic argument that the two complexes are truly separate machines.

interactions.mechanism: PIP3 made by PI3K binds SIN1 and releases its hold on the kinase site - so growth-factor signalling switches mTORC2 on, not only mTORC1.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.
interactions.note: Thin - one supporting study for a step drawn as canonical.

interactions.mechanism: PTEN erases PIP3, undoing PI3K. Losing PTEN is one of the commonest ways a tumour switches this whole axis on permanently.
interactions.teaching_note: PTEN does not touch the PI3K protein. It removes PI3K's product. Drawn as an inhibition arrow for readability — the mechanism is enzymatic reversal.

interactions.mechanism: SGK1 is a second mTORC2 substrate alongside Akt, and it carries some of the functions usually credited to Akt.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.

interactions.mechanism: The first job ever assigned to mTORC2 was shaping the cell's skeleton - and it was noticed precisely because rapamycin did not block it.
interactions.note: Historically this is how mTORC2 was discovered as a separate thing.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC2 drives lipid synthesis and this is a substantial part of how it supports tumour growth.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.

interactions.mechanism: Prostate tumours driven by Pten loss need mTORC2 specifically - normal prostate does not. A real therapeutic window, at least in mice.
DEPTOR sits on mTOR and damps both complexes; myeloma cells overexpress it and depend on that damping.

The TSC complex is the pathway's main tumour suppressor. Inherit one broken copy and lesions grow wherever the second copy is lost - the clearest human evidence that mTORC1 activity drives tissue overgrowth.
interactions.teaching_note: A deliberate shortcut edge: TSC never touches mTORC1. It acts on Rheb. Shown so the overview reads cleanly; switch to Research level to see the two-step version.
interactions.context_note: Deliberately compressed: TSC acts on Rheb, never on mTORC1. Kept as one link so the overview reads cleanly.
interactions.note: This is the edge that turns the biochemistry into a disease.

interactions.mechanism: Hyperactive mTORC1 reprograms translation toward a specific set of pro-growth and pro-metastasis mRNAs - the tumour becomes addicted to that programme.
Everolimus is rapamycin with a solubilising side chain - same FKBP12 mechanism, better oral pharmacokinetics. It is the molecule that carried this pathway into routine clinical use.
interactions.note: Six trials behind one arrow - by far the best-evidenced edge in the Atlas.

interactions.mechanism: Temsirolimus is the intravenous rapamycin analogue, and the first mTOR inhibitor to show a survival benefit in a randomised trial.
RECORD-1: everolimus roughly doubled progression-free survival after other targeted therapy failed.
interactions.boundary: Second-line setting, after VEGF-targeted therapy - not first-line.

interactions.mechanism: In poor-prognosis renal cancer, temsirolimus improved overall survival against interferon - the hardest endpoint there is.
interactions.boundary: Poor-prognosis patients specifically; the combination arm did not beat temsirolimus alone.
interactions.note: Overall survival, not a surrogate. Worth pointing at.

interactions.mechanism: RADIANT-3: progression-free survival more than doubled in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.
BOLERO-2: adding everolimus to hormone therapy roughly doubled progression-free survival in hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer.
interactions.boundary: Progression-free survival, in combination with exemestane - overall survival was not significantly improved.
interactions.note: Say PFS, not survival. The distinction is the whole argument of this Atlas.

interactions.mechanism: EXIST trials: everolimus shrank the brain tumours (SEGA) and kidney lesions of tuberous sclerosis - treating the genetic cause of mTORC1 hyperactivation rather than a symptom.
interactions.boundary: Lesions regrow when the drug is stopped - this is suppression, not cure.
interactions.note: The purest case in the Atlas: known gene, known pathway, matched drug, randomised evidence.

interactions.mechanism: EXIST-2 tested everolimus against renal ANGIOMYOLIPOMA in patients with tuberous sclerosis or sporadic LAM, and shrank those lesions by >=50% in 42% versus 0% on placebo.
interactions.boundary: Scope: the endpoint was the kidney lesion, not LAM lung disease. The evidence that mTOR inhibition treats the lung disease itself is the MILES trial with sirolimus - see the RAPA-LAM edge.

interactions.mechanism: Counter-intuitive but well tested: low-dose mTOR inhibition improved vaccine response and cut infections in elderly volunteers. The same drug class that suppresses transplant rejection can enhance an ageing immune system at a lower dose.
interactions.boundary: Dose-dependent and duration-dependent - this is not the immunosuppressive regimen. MAN2021's larger follow-up did not reproduce the clinical infection benefit.
interactions.context_note: Direction depends on dose and schedule. Transplant-level dosing is immunosuppressive; intermittent low dosing improved vaccine responses in older adults. Treating this as one effect with one sign is the error.
interactions.note: THE dose-dependence case study, and a genuine apparent contradiction with the drug's immunosuppressant label. Prime Contradiction Engine seed.

interactions.mechanism: Blocking mTOR reversed Akt-driven pre-cancerous prostate lesions in mice, showing the growth was mTORC1-dependent and reversible.

The pathway's principal negative feedback loop. Sustained S6K1 activity phosphorylates IRS-1 and represses its expression, so the insulin receptor can no longer signal to PI3K. This is the main reason blocking mTOR paradoxically RAISES Akt activity, and a major contributor to rapalog-associated insulin resistance.
interactions.teaching_note: The pathway's most clinically consequential feedback loop: blocking mTORC1 releases IRS-1, reactivating PI3K/Akt. Half of why rapalog monotherapy underperforms.
interactions.boundary: Established in cells and mouse genetics. Its contribution to rapalog dysglycaemia in humans, relative to mTORC2 loss, has not been apportioned.

interactions.mechanism: IRS proteins are the adaptors that carry the signal from the insulin/IGF-1 receptor to PI3K. Deplete them and the receptor is still there but the wire is cut.

ERK phosphorylates TSC2 and inactivates the TSC complex, so Ras-MAPK growth signalling converges on the same brake that Akt releases. This is the third upstream arm alongside PI3K/Akt and AMPK, and clinically it is a route to mTORC1 activation that PI3K inhibitors do not close.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus; Roux 2004 describes the parallel RSK arm and is not yet held.

interactions.mechanism: A second feedback arm: inhibiting mTORC1 releases a PI3K-dependent brake and MAPK signalling goes up. Together with S6K1-IRS1 this is why single-agent mTOR inhibition tends to be met by compensatory growth signalling.
interactions.teaching_note: The second feedback arm. mTORC1 inhibition activates ERK PI3K-dependently, which is the rationale for combined mTOR/MEK strategies.
interactions.boundary: Single-study edge in this corpus.

interactions.mechanism: Metformin also inhibits mTORC1 WITHOUT going through AMPK: the effect survives in AMPK-null and TSC1/2-null cells and instead requires the Rag GTPases. This is the arm usually left out of the 'metformin works via AMPK' summary.
interactions.boundary: Runs in parallel with METFORMIN-AMPK, not instead of it. The relative weight of the two routes in humans is unresolved.
interactions.context_note: Dose is the whole argument. Concentrations used in cell culture are typically far above plasma levels achieved at clinical doses, so in vitro mechanism may not describe what metformin does in a patient.

interactions.mechanism: The only edge in this Atlas connecting an amino-acid sensor to an organismal ageing phenotype. Losing Drosophila Sestrin produces fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle degeneration and cardiac malfunction - all prevented by inhibiting TOR or activating AMPK.
interactions.boundary: Fly only, and the readout is age-related pathology rather than lifespan. No mammalian sensor-to-ageing evidence exists.

interactions.mechanism: The MILES trial: sirolimus stabilised lung function (FEV1) in lymphangioleiomyomatosis while patients took it, and decline resumed after stopping. This - not the everolimus angiomyolipoma trial - is the evidence that mTOR inhibition treats LAM lung disease.
interactions.boundary: Benefit is suppressive: lung function declined again after withdrawal.

interactions.mechanism: Renal cancers frequently carry lesions that leave mTORC1 constitutively active - which is why this tissue responds to mTOR inhibitors at all, and why an exceptional responder could be traced to TSC1 loss.
interactions.teaching_note: Association, not demonstrated causation. Renal cancers often carry lesions that leave mTORC1 active; that is why the tissue responds to rapalogs, not proof that mTORC1 initiates the disease.
interactions.boundary: Correlative plus one n-of-1 genomic case (IYE2012); not a demonstration that mTORC1 activation initiates RCC.

interactions.mechanism: Nuclear TFEB switches on the lysosomal and autophagy gene programme as a single coordinated module, expanding the lysosomal compartment.
interactions.teaching_note: This is the arm that makes the pathway circular. mTORC1 controls TFEB, TFEB controls how many lysosomes exist, and lysosomes are where mTORC1 is controlled.
interactions.boundary: Transcriptional output measured as gene expression and lysosomal markers; how much the compartment actually expands varies with cell type and starvation depth.

interactions.mechanism: A larger, renewed lysosomal compartment changes the platform on which mTORC1 is regulated — the return leg of the lysosome-to-nucleus circuit.
interactions.teaching_note: Closing this arm turns a dangling output into a real feedback loop. Before it was curated, the map could not show that mTORC1 shapes its own regulatory surface.
interactions.boundary: SET2012 establishes lysosome-to-nucleus signalling via mTOR and TFEB; the quantitative effect of compartment size on mTORC1 output is not resolved.

interactions.mechanism: Genome-wide CRISPR screens identify at least two parallel relays carrying mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1: AMPK, and the heme-regulated inhibitor HRI acting through the integrated stress response.
interactions.teaching_note: Multitiered by design. The cell does not read mitochondrial failure through one channel, which is why single-gene knockouts rarely abolish the response.
interactions.boundary: CRISPR screening in cell lines; the relative weight of the AMPK and HRI arms in tissue is untested.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC1 raises mitochondrial respiratory capacity through a YY1–PGC-1α transcriptional programme and through 4E-BP-dependent translation of respiratory components.
interactions.teaching_note: One of the few places mTORC1 acts mainly through transcription. Adipose Raptor knockout raising respiration (POL2008) is the genetic confirmation that this is not a rapamycin artefact.
interactions.boundary: Effect size varies strongly by tissue; the transcriptional and translational arms have not been cleanly separated in vivo.

interactions.mechanism: mTOR interacts with YY1 and is required for the YY1–PGC-1α complex to drive mitochondrial gene expression; rapamycin lowers both the transcripts and oxygen consumption.
interactions.teaching_note: A nuclear action of a kinase usually taught as cytosolic. The pathway is not confined to the lysosomal surface and the cytosol.
interactions.boundary: Single-study support in this corpus for the direct interaction; the downstream respiratory phenotype is better replicated than the binding itself.

interactions.mechanism: Unleashing mTORC1 by deleting TSC1 drives quiescent haematopoietic stem cells into cycle, raises mitochondrial biogenesis and floods them with ROS; an antioxidant rescues self-renewal.
interactions.teaching_note: The antioxidant rescue is what makes this causal rather than correlative — ROS is the mediator, not a side observation.
interactions.boundary: Demonstrated in haematopoietic stem cells, where quiescence is the baseline state. Cell types that are already cycling need not behave this way.

interactions.mechanism: Oxidative stress activates a redox-sensitive PI3K–Akt–mTORC1–eIF4A cascade that selectively promotes cap-dependent translation of P-glycoprotein.
interactions.teaching_note: Together with mTORC1 → ROS this closes a positive feedback loop. Positive loops behave completely differently from negative ones: they amplify rather than stabilise, which is how a transient oxidative insult can become a persistent state.
interactions.boundary: One cell-line study in a multidrug-resistance context; whether the loop runs in normal physiology at these ROS levels is untested.

interactions.mechanism: mTORC2–Akt signalling localises to mitochondria-associated ER membranes and regulates mitochondrial physiology from there.
interactions.teaching_note: Direct evidence that mTOR signalling happens at more than one membrane. The lysosome is where mTORC1 is switched on; it is not the only place mTOR works.
interactions.boundary: Biochemical fractionation and imaging in cell lines; the functional contribution relative to plasma-membrane mTORC2 is not quantified.

interactions.mechanism: Akt phosphorylates FOXO transcription factors and excludes them from the nucleus. Rictor or mLST8 deletion abolishes signalling to Akt–FOXO while sparing S6K1.
interactions.teaching_note: The clean genetic separation: this arm belongs to mTORC2, not mTORC1. It also means rapamycin does not release FOXO the way an mTOR kinase inhibitor can.
interactions.boundary: Mouse knockouts and cell lines; FOXO isoform contributions differ by tissue.

interactions.mechanism: TOR signalling and rapamycin influence lifespan partly through the SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO transcriptional programmes.
interactions.teaching_note: An invertebrate result. It is the mechanistic basis most often cited for 'mTOR inhibition acts through stress-resistance programmes', and it has not been shown in mammals in this corpus.
interactions.boundary: C. elegans only. DAF-16 is the FOXO orthologue; mapping worm lifespan genetics onto mammalian FOXO1/3 is an inference, not a demonstration.

interactions.mechanism: mTOR inhibition reverses Akt-driven prostate intraepithelial neoplasia partly through HIF-1-dependent pathways, placing HIF-1α downstream of mTORC1 in this setting.
interactions.teaching_note: Note the direction. Hypoxia → HIF-1α is the arm everyone expects, but it is mTORC1 → HIF-1α that this corpus supports; the hypoxia arm is drawn here through REDD1 instead, because that is what the cited paper shows.
interactions.boundary: Mouse prostate model with pharmacological mTOR inhibition; HIF-1α is one of several pathways implicated in the same experiment.

routes.name: Amino acids → mTORC1
routes.summary: How a cell tastes leucine, arginine and methionine — and why the answer is three different sensors converging on one lysosome.
routes.story: Follow the highlighted spine: leucine switches off a brake (Sestrin2), which switches off a second brake (GATOR2 on GATOR1), which frees the Rag GTPases to drag mTORC1 to the lysosome. Nothing here activates the kinase — the amino-acid route only decides where mTORC1 sits. Rheb does the switching on.

steps.what: Leucine binds Sestrin2 — and switches a brake off.
steps.why: Sestrin2 carries a pocket that fits leucine with roughly 20 µM affinity. That number is the whole argument: it sits inside the range over which leucine inside a real cell actually rises and falls, so Sestrin2 changes state when leucine changes, rather than being permanently full or permanently empty.
steps.changed: Leucine-loaded Sestrin2 can no longer hold onto GATOR2. Nothing has been switched on yet — something has been let go of.
steps.consequence: GATOR2 is now free. Watch what it does with that freedom: it does not activate anything either. It inhibits the next brake.
steps.certainty: The binding is structurally resolved and the affinity measured in vitro. What is not established is whether the same 20 µM setpoint holds in tissues with different leucine transport — so this is high mechanistic confidence with unproven human physiological calibration.
steps.matters: This is where the pathway's logic starts being counter-intuitive. The cell does not detect food and then send a 'grow' signal. It detects food and stops sending a 'do not grow' signal. Almost every nutrient input works this way, and it is the reason the pathway is so hard to read off a diagram of arrows.

steps.what: GATOR2 is released — the first brake comes off.
steps.why: Sestrin2 and GATOR2 are mutually exclusive binding partners: leucine-bound Sestrin2 lets go, and free GATOR2 becomes able to act on GATOR1.
steps.changed: GATOR2 goes from sequestered to available. Its availability, not its abundance, is what the cell regulates.
steps.consequence: Available GATOR2 now inhibits GATOR1. Count the negatives as you go — you are two into a chain of them.
steps.certainty: Mechanistically solid and reproduced. Structures of the GATOR2 cage and its sensor-binding surfaces exist; the cited corpus evidence here is cell-line biochemistry, so human relevance is plausible rather than demonstrated.
steps.matters: Regulation by sequestration rather than by synthesis is fast and cheap — no transcription, no translation, no degradation. It lets the cell respond to a meal in seconds instead of hours. Evolution reaches for this trick whenever speed matters.

steps.what: GATOR2 shuts down GATOR1 — the second brake comes off.
steps.why: GATOR1 is the machine that switches the Rag GTPases off. GATOR2 inhibits it. So inhibiting GATOR1 means the Rags stop being switched off.
steps.changed: GATOR1's GAP activity toward RagA/B falls. Two negatives have now cancelled: leucine present → Sestrin2 inhibited → GATOR2 free → GATOR1 inhibited.
steps.consequence: The Rag GTPases can finally load GTP and stay loaded. That is the state that does something.
steps.certainty: Everyone agrees the inhibition happens; nobody has fully resolved how it happens catalytically. This step is graded emerging consensus with medium mechanistic confidence — an honest hole in the middle of a canonical pathway.
steps.matters: Worth pausing on: this is a textbook step that a textbook will draw as a confident arrow, and the mechanism behind it is genuinely unresolved. A map that hides that is more comfortable and less useful.

steps.what: With GATOR1 suppressed, the Rag GTPases stay loaded with GTP.
steps.why: GATOR1 is a GAP — it forces RagA/B to hydrolyse GTP to GDP. Remove the GAP and RagA/B accumulates in the GTP state, which is its active conformation.
steps.changed: RagA/B flips from GDP-loaded to GTP-loaded. Note the inversion in this heterodimer: RagA/B is active with GTP, but its partner RagC/D is active with GDP.
steps.consequence: GTP-loaded RagA/B can now grip Raptor. That grip is what brings mTORC1 in.
steps.certainty: The GAP activity is directly demonstrated biochemistry, and human genetics supports its physiological importance — DEPDC5 mutations cause focal epilepsy. The cited corpus evidence is cell-line work, so human relevance is graded plausible.
steps.matters: Nucleotide state is the pathway's memory. A GTPase holds its answer until something actively changes it, which lets a signal that arrived seconds ago still be true now.

steps.what: Ragulator holds the Rags on the lysosomal membrane.
steps.why: The Rags are not free-floating. Ragulator is lipid-anchored to the lysosome and clamps the Rag heterodimer to that surface, so everything the Rags do, they do at one specific place.
steps.changed: Nothing about the Rags' activity changes here. What is fixed is their address.
steps.consequence: Because the Rags are on the lysosome, whatever they recruit arrives on the lysosome too.
steps.certainty: The tethering role is well established. Ragulator has also been reported as a GEF for RagA/B; that assignment is less secure than the tethering function, and the model records the tethering claim rather than the GEF claim.
steps.matters: This is the step that makes the rest of the pathway make sense. Signalling here is not chemistry in free solution — it is a set of mechanisms for putting particular molecules in particular places. Location is the regulated variable.

steps.what: The Rags recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome. They do not switch it on.
steps.why: GTP-loaded RagA/B binds Raptor directly, dragging the whole mTORC1 complex out of the cytosol and onto the lysosomal surface.
steps.changed: mTORC1's location changes, and only its location. Its kinase activity at this moment is essentially unchanged. Recruitment is not activation — these are two different claims and this map draws them differently on purpose.
steps.consequence: mTORC1 is now in the one place where it can meet Rheb. Meeting Rheb is the event that actually switches it on.
steps.certainty: Directly demonstrated and reproduced across labs; the corpus evidence is cell-line biochemistry, so human relevance is graded plausible rather than established.
steps.matters: If you take one thing from this route, take this: amino acids alone cannot make a cell grow. Starve a cell of growth factors, flood it with leucine, and mTORC1 will sit on the lysosome doing nothing. The nutrient arm answers 'are the parts available?' — it does not answer 'am I allowed to build?'

steps.what: Rheb switches mTORC1 on — and only growth factors control Rheb.
steps.why: GTP-loaded Rheb binds mTORC1 and physically realigns its active site into a catalytically competent conformation. This is an allosteric activation, a different kind of event from everything upstream in this route.
steps.changed: mTORC1 becomes an active kinase. Now, and only now, S6K1 and 4E-BP1 start getting phosphorylated.
steps.consequence: The cell builds. And because Rheb is controlled by the TSC complex, which is controlled by Akt, AMPK and ERK, the growth-factor and energy arms all converge on this single step.
steps.certainty: Structurally resolved and mechanistically secure. Cited evidence is mammalian cell work, so human relevance is graded plausible.
steps.matters: This is coincidence detection, and it is the answer to why the pathway is built the way it is. Two independent conditions — nutrients supplying location, growth factors supplying activation — must both be satisfied at the same place and the same time. A cell that grew on either signal alone would build without materials or build when told not to. The lysosome is where the cell checks both answers against each other.

routes.name: Growth factors → mTORC1
routes.summary: Insulin and IGF-1 do not push the accelerator. They release two brakes - and then mTORC1 immediately builds two brakes of its own.
routes.story: Two negatives in a row: Akt disables TSC, TSC stops disabling Rheb, Rheb switches mTORC1 on. Then follow the arrows that come back. mTORC1 switches on S6K1, and S6K1 phosphorylates and represses IRS-1 - cutting the wire between the insulin receptor and PI3K. That is the pathway's principal negative feedback loop, and it is the main reason mTOR inhibitors paradoxically raise Akt activity. Grb10 is a second, parallel arm of the same idea, and mTORC1 inhibition also relieves a brake on MAPK. Note too that ERK enters from the right onto TSC2: growth signalling reaches mTORC1 through Ras-MAPK as well as through Akt, which is why PI3K inhibitors alone rarely close the pathway.

routes.name: Rapamycin — what it actually blocks
routes.summary: One drug, two complexes, and a time axis. Most confusion about rapamycin comes from ignoring the third of those.
routes.story: The drug is a two-part molecule: rapamycin alone does nothing, rapamycin+FKBP12 blocks mTORC1 — but only partially, which is why 4E-BP1 stays half-phosphorylated. The dashed arrow to mTORC2 is the one everyone gets wrong: it does not exist acutely, only after days of exposure. That single time-dependence separates the benefit from the side effect.

routes.name: mTORC1 → outputs → phenotype
routes.summary: Where the signalling stops being signalling. Five branches leave mTORC1, and they do not share a fate: rapamycin blocks some completely, others barely at all.
routes.story: Follow the spine: mTORC1 releases 4E-BP1, 4E-BP1 lets go of eIF4E, translation runs, muscle is built. Then look at what does not follow that line. Rapamycin blocks S6K1 almost completely but 4E-BP1 only partly - which is why 'mTORC1 activity' measured as p-S6K can look abolished while half the real output carries on. And the two lifespan arrows point in opposite directions: losing S6K1 extends life, keeping 4E-BP active extends life. One node is not the pathway.

routes.name: Energy & stress → mTORC1
routes.summary: The third input. Nutrients say what is available and growth factors say whether to bother; stress overrides both.
routes.story: Three different stresses, three different speeds. AMPK reads falling ATP in seconds. REDD1 needs low oxygen to switch on a gene, so it is minutes. The integrated stress response is slower still. All three converge on the same two brakes - and notice AMPK does not only lift the brake on autophagy, it pushes ULK1 directly. That is the pathway doing arithmetic rather than relaying. One caveat on the left-hand corner: metformin is drawn into AMPK because that is the route it is usually credited to, but the dashed arrow running past AMPK straight to mTORC1 is real - metformin still works in AMPK-null and LKB1-null tissue. How the two routes divide the labour in people is unresolved.

routes.name: The mTORC2 branch
routes.summary: The same kinase, a different set of partners, and almost none of the same drugs. Half the mTOR story, usually told as a footnote to rapamycin's side effects.
routes.story: mLST8 is the clean argument that these really are two machines: delete it and mTORC2 dies while mTORC1 carries on. Everything below mTORC2 was discovered because rapamycin failed to block it - the actin cytoskeleton first. And the dashed arrow from rapamycin is the whole clinical problem in one line: absent acutely, present after days.

routes.name: From pathway to clinic
routes.summary: The only route here where the badges are mostly B. mTOR drugs already work in people - just not yet for the reason this Atlas cares most about.
routes.story: Read this route next to the amino-acid one and the contrast is the point. There, almost every badge is D. Here they are B - randomised human trials, one of them (temsirolimus in renal cancer) on overall survival. The pathway is not unproven in people. Watch the two arrows into LAM, though: everolimus was tested against the kidney lesion in EXIST-2, while the lung disease itself was treated with sirolimus in MILES. They are different drugs and different endpoints, and collapsing them is a common error. What remains unproven is the longevity claim: every arrow on this page ends in a tumour or an immune endpoint, and not one of them ends in lifespan.

loops.sign_caveat: Sign is the parity of inhibitory steps around the loop. It says which direction the loop pushes, not how strongly — loop strength depends on the relative weight of each arm, which is cell-type dependent.
loops.name: AMPK ↔ ULK1 set-point
loops.why: ULK1 phosphorylates the very kinase that activated it. So 'AMPK switches on autophagy' is not an arrow but a loop with a set-point, and the steady state depends on the relative strength of both directions.

loops.sign_caveat: Sign is the parity of inhibitory steps around the loop. It says which direction the loop pushes, not how strongly — loop strength depends on the relative weight of each arm, which is cell-type dependent.
loops.name: Reactive oxygen species → mTORC1 → Reactive oxygen species

loops.sign_caveat: Sign is the parity of inhibitory steps around the loop. It says which direction the loop pushes, not how strongly — loop strength depends on the relative weight of each arm, which is cell-type dependent.
loops.name: mTORC1 → MAPK feedback
loops.why: mTORC1 inhibition relieves feedback and activates ERK in a PI3K-dependent way. This is the rationale for combining mTOR with MEK inhibition rather than escalating mTOR inhibition alone.

loops.why: The second arm of negative feedback onto the receptor. mTORC1 phosphorylation stabilises Grb10, which damps insulin/IGF-1 receptor signalling.

loops.name: S6K1 → IRS-1 feedback
loops.why: The pathway's most clinically consequential loop. mTORC1 drives S6K1, S6K1 degrades IRS-1, and PI3K signalling falls. Block mTORC1 and IRS-1 is spared, so Akt reactivates — half the reason rapalog monotherapy underperforms.

open_loops.name: mTORC1 → autophagy → nutrient supply → mTORC1
open_loops.why: Autophagy regenerates amino acids, which feed the very sensors that control mTORC1. This is a real homeostatic loop and the Atlas holds both halves as separate arms, but no curated edge for autophagy-derived amino acids re-entering the sensing machinery.

open_localisations.name: Golgi as an mTORC1 activation site
open_localisations.why: Proposed in the amino-acid-transporter literature (GOB2016 reviews the idea that intracellular transporters mark the site of activation), but no study in this corpus demonstrates mTORC1 activation at the Golgi. Adding the edge would assert more than the citations support. Closing this gap needs a primary paper in the corpus, at which point the edge appears automatically.

open_localisations.name: Subcellular mTOR pools beyond the lysosome
open_localisations.why: Live BRET biosensor imaging (BOU2020) reads mTOR activity separately in cytosol, on the lysosomal surface, in the nucleus and near mitochondria — so mTOR signalling is measurably not one pool. This map represents the peri-mitochondrial case concretely (mTORC2 at MAM, BET2013) and the nuclear case functionally (mTORC1 to YY1–PGC-1α), but it does not yet model the pools as separate entities with their own activity states.
